newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: SE Asia grain trade shrugs off U.S. mad cow report.
newsitem.headline: SE Asia grain trade shrugs off U.S. mad cow report.

text.p: After initial nervousness on a jittery Chicago market overnight, Asian commodity traders reacted sceptically on Thursday to a U.S. report an Indiana rose grower may have died from the human version of mad cow disease.

Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME) live cattle futures ended limit down on Wednesday and Chicago agriculture futures were also sold on a wire report that the Indiana man had died of Creutzfeldt-Jacob Disease (CJD).

"I think the market's pretty nervous about this. The implications are pretty serious," a dealer for a U.S. commodity company said, adding the news could affect U.S. cattle exports and sales of U.S. corn, soybeans and soymeal.
Other dealers quickly discounted the report.

"I don't believe it is BSE (bovine spongiform encephalopathy)," a dealer for a European trading house said, referring to the scientific name for mad cow disease. "It's a random disease. I don't really see any impact in the market."
"I don't think it's true so there's no point in speculating at this time," another dealer in a commodity firm here said.
An international consumer panic was triggered about the safety of beef when a new strain of CJD was linked to BSE in British cattle last year.
A report from the U.S. Center for Disease Control (CDC) that CJD deaths were very rare in the U.S. and are not linked to mad cow disease helped calm the market.

"I think we can now safely ignore the report. By tomorrow morning, people will wonder why they were so worried about it. It's not the same type of strain they saw in the U.K. At the end of the day, its a lot of ado about nothing," one analyst said.
The U.S. CJD report came out a few weeks after an outbreak of hog foot-and-mouth disease in Taiwan demolished the multibillion dollar pork export industry there.
Taiwan's pork industry will take years to recover after Japan and Korea, which imports most of its pork from the island, slapped an indefinite ban on Taiwanese pork products.
The grains and oilseeds business in the region, however, remained quiet with most waiting for release of the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) export sales figures on Friday.
"There hasn't been a lot of interest in corn or meal lately," one trader said.
"It's pretty quiet. Those who scrambled earlier for nearbys have already done so. We may see countries in the region taking a look next week at corn and meal," another dealer said.
The trade was also looking at some open positions in June for soymeal in Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia.

Dealers estimate Indonesia may be looking for about 40,000 tonnes of meal although one placed it at about 80,000-100,000 tonnes. Malaysia and Thailand were both said to be sniffing around for 20,000 tonnes of soymeal each.
"I think people will be trading more on the USDA export sales report tomorrow," one analyst said.
Chinese corn continued to be offered in the region, but buyers were scarce and most people were content to wait for prices to ease before stepping back into the market.
Chinese and Argentine corn offers are maintaining their discounts to U.S. origin.

Chinese and Argentine corn were both seen by the trade at US$147-$150 a tonne C&F for May/July shipment on a Panamax or a Handy vessel while U.S. corn fetched a quote of about $152-$154 a tonne C&F for May/June on a Panamax.
